quartiers:Le Marais.name: Le Marais
quartiers:Le Marais.teaser: A drained marsh that became the court's address, was left to rot, and was saved by being too poor to rebuild
quartiers:Le Marais.story: Marais means marsh, and it was one: wet ground on the Right Bank that the Knights Templar and the religious orders began draining after Louis VII granted the Templars land here in 1139. Nobles moved in once the royal square went up in 1612, built stone mansions round private courtyards, then followed the court to Versailles and left it to workshops and decay. Too poor to rebuild, it kept its houses. In 1964 André Malraux made the Marais France's first protected 'secteur sauvegardé'. Push a carriage gate and you find a 17th-century courtyard; Rue des Rosiers is still the Jewish Pletzl.
quartiers:Le Marais.why: Walk with your head up and push every open carriage door: the mansions show their faces to the courtyard, not the street.
facts: Hôtels particuliers, the Pletzl around Rue des Rosiers, the Carnavalet and Picasso museums
Weekday mornings, before the Saturday shopping crowd fills the lanes
Place des Vosges (its own card); the 17th-century Marché des Enfants Rouges on Rue de Bretagne burned on 12 Oct 2026 (its own card)
L'As du Fallafel, Breizh Café, Datil, Parcelles (all in the tables)

quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.name: Canal Saint-Martin
quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.teaser: Nine locks and iron footbridges on a canal paid for by a tax on wine
quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.story: In 1802 Paris drank from the same Seine it emptied its sewage into, and cholera and dysentery followed. Napoleon ordered a canal to bring clean water from the Ourcq and float in grain and stone, paid for with a tax on wine. The canal opened in 1825, four years after his death. Under Napoleon III about half of it was roofed over; Boulevard Richard-Lenoir runs on top. In the open stay 4.5 km of locks and footbridges, where Amélie skips stones in the 2001 film, and the Hôtel du Nord of the 1938 film and its cry of 'Atmosphère !'.
quartiers:Canal Saint-Martin.why: Come on a fine Sunday evening and sit on the stone edge with the neighbourhood while a boat works up through a lock.
facts: The locks, the footbridges and the 10th at its aperitif on the quays
A boat rising through one of the double locks; the Hôtel du Nord on Quai de Jemmapes
Du Pain et des Idées for bread, Ten Belles for coffee, Le Pavillon des Canaux to linger (their own cards)

quartiers:Belleville.name: Belleville
quartiers:Belleville.teaser: The steep village Paris annexed in 1860, now Chinatown, North Africa and street art on one slope
quartiers:Belleville.story: Belleville was vineyards and open-air guinguettes, drinking gardens beyond the city's tax wall, until Paris annexed it in 1860. Haussmann's demolitions pushed the workers of the centre up here, and wave after wave of newcomers followed: Jewish, North African, then Chinese, whose restaurants and grocers now line the boulevard at the foot of the hill. Édith Piaf grew up singing in these streets. Climb on through the painted walls of Rue Dénoyez to the terraced Parc de Belleville, opened in 1988 on a hill of about 108 m, where the whole of Paris lies flat below you to the west.
quartiers:Belleville.why: Climb to the top of Parc de Belleville for the free view west, then come down through the street-art lanes.
facts: Chinese and North African food streets, street art and the hilltop view
Late afternoon for the view from the park terrace
The Parc de Belleville terrace; the plaque at 72 Rue de Belleville
Le Baratin (in the tables); coffee at Belleville Brûlerie (its own card)

quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.name: Montmartre
quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.teaser: Paris's highest hill at about 130 m: a martyr's name, gypsum mines and a basilica built as penance
quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.story: The hill's name is a legend: Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris, is said to have been beheaded up here around 250 AD, and Mont des Martyrs stuck. The ground is real enough: Montmartre was quarried for gypsum, the stone behind 'plaster of Paris', until the mines wound down around the time Paris annexed the village in 1860. Cheap rents then brought Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec, Van Gogh and Picasso. Sacré-Cœur was begun in 1875 as national penance after the defeat by Prussia and the bloodshed of the Commune. Climb the stairs from the Abbesses side, skip the easels of Place du Tertre, and keep to the back lanes behind the basilica.
quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.why: Come up by the stairs and the back streets, not the funicular crowd, and look north from behind the basilica as well as south.
facts: The stairs, the back lanes, the view and the bohemian story
Early morning, before the coaches reach Place du Tertre
The Musée de Montmartre and the Clos Montmartre vineyard (their own cards)
Bouillon Pigalle at the foot of the hill (in the tables); a drink at Le Rooftop, Terrass'' Hotel (its own card)

quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.teaser: A quarter grown round a 6th-century royal abbey, long before its cafés became famous
quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.story: The quarter is named for an abbey. Childebert I, son of Clovis, founded it in the mid-6th century to hold the relics he brought back from the siege of Zaragoza, among them a fragment of the True Cross and Saint Vincent's tunic. The church was consecrated in 558, the year the king died, and it became the burial place of the Merovingian kings. The present church, its nave Romanesque, stands on that foundation. What most visitors never hear is that for centuries the abbey's annual fair, the Foire Saint-Germain, made this one of Europe's great marketplaces. Publishers still cluster around it.
quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.why: Go inside the abbey church before you take a café terrace: it is the reason the quarter exists at all.
facts: The abbey church, bookshops and publishers' streets, the old cafés
Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots, and the post-war cellars told in the chanson story (their own cards)
Brasserie Lipp, Polidor, Le Relais de l'Entrecôte (all in the tables)

quartiers:Place des Vosges.name: Place des Vosges
quartiers:Place des Vosges.teaser: Paris's first planned square, built where a king died of a lance through his visor
quartiers:Place des Vosges.story: Here stood the Hôtel des Tournelles, the royal residence where Henri II died in 1559 after a lance splinter went through his visor in a tournament; Catherine de' Medici had it pulled down. There Henri IV built a square from 1605 to 1612 and ordered every front to follow one design: 36 pavilions of red brick and pale stone over vaulted arcades round a garden of limes and four fountains. Opened in 1612 as the Place Royale, it took the name of the Vosges in 1800, the first department to pay its taxes to the Republic. Victor Hugo lived at no. 6 from 1832 to 1848.
quartiers:Place des Vosges.why: Walk the whole arcade round once, then sit in the garden: the matching fronts only read as one design from the middle.
facts: Between the 3rd and 4th arrondissements, in the Marais
The square and its arcades are free and always open; Maison de Victor Hugo at no. 6 is closed Mondays (seen Jul 2026)
Free; the Maison de Victor Hugo's permanent collection is also free (seen Jul 2026)
About an hour with the Hugo apartment
Hugo's apartment at no. 6; the walk through the arcades at dusk when the shops close

quartiers:Place Dauphine.name: Place Dauphine
quartiers:Place Dauphine.teaser: A quiet triangle of houses on the prow of the Île de la Cité, shaped by a sandbank
quartiers:Place Dauphine.story: Henri IV's second royal square is a triangle for a plain reason: it fills the silt spit at the downstream tip of the Île de la Cité, next to his new Pont Neuf. On 10 March 1607 he handed the land, about three acres, to Achille de Harlay on one condition, that every façade repeat the same model, and named it for the Dauphin, his six-year-old son and the future Louis XIII. The last house was finished in 1616. Many fronts have been altered since, but the shape and the quiet survive: step in from the bridge and the traffic noise drops away.
quartiers:Place Dauphine.why: Walk in from the Pont Neuf end at lunchtime: two minutes from the busiest bridge in Paris and you can hear the gravel underfoot.
facts: Western tip of the Île de la Cité, entered from the Pont Neuf or Rue de Harlay, 1st
Weekday lunchtime or a summer evening
Twenty minutes, longer with a terrace
The Square du Vert-Galant, down the steps below the bridge (its own card)

quartiers:Place des Victoires.name: Place des Victoires
quartiers:Place des Victoires.teaser: A round square built by a courtier to flatter Louis XIV, now ringed by fashion houses
quartiers:Place des Victoires.story: This is the royal square no king built. After the Treaty of Nijmegen, the Maréchal de la Feuillade commissioned a gilded statue of Louis XIV, then hired Jules Hardouin-Mansart to raise a whole circular square around it in 1685 and 1686. The approaching streets were set slightly off line so the king's figure would always stand clear against the façades. The Dauphin inaugurated it in March 1686, standing in for his absent father. The original statue, a standing king crowned by Victory, was melted down in the Revolution; the rearing horseman you see now is François-Joseph Bosio's replacement of 1822. Today the ground floors hold fashion boutiques.
quartiers:Place des Victoires.why: Walk in from one of the side streets and watch the horseman come clear against the curved fronts, exactly as planned.
facts: Between the 1st and 2nd arrondissements, a few minutes north of the Palais-Royal
Morning light on the curved façades
Bosio's 1822 bronze; the Palais-Royal garden nearby (its own card)

curiosities:The empire of the dead.name: The empire of the dead
curiosities:The empire of the dead.teaser: Over the door a line still warns: 'Arrête ! C'est ici l'empire de la Mort'
curiosities:The empire of the dead.story: Paris's cemeteries were overflowing by the 1780s, and from 1786 the bones were carted, by night, into the old limestone quarries under the Left Bank. Workers stacked femurs and skulls into walls, and over the threshold of the ossuary they carved a warning: 'Arrête ! C'est ici l'empire de la Mort', Stop, here is the empire of the dead. Today you go down about 20 m and some 130 steps, walk roughly 1.5 km of cold, damp galleries, and come up again by another stair. The site reopened in April 2026 after renovation work, with a headset sound guide replacing the old audioguide.
curiosities:The empire of the dead.why: Book a timed slot before you go; there is no walk-in, and reading the carved warning in the dark is the moment.
facts: Catacombes de Paris, Place Denfert-Rochereau, 14th: timed online booking only; full price €31, reduced €25, headset included (Oct 2026, Paris Musées press kit and press reports; check catacombes.paris.fr); closed Mondays
The step count (130 or 131) and the reduced and child prices differ between listings; the number of dead (usually given as about six million) is an estimate

curiosities:Guimard's metro, 1900.name: Guimard's glass dragonflies
curiosities:Guimard's metro, 1900.teaser: Two of Guimard's glass-roofed metro pavilions survive, and one of them has moved
curiosities:Guimard's metro, 1900.story: The metro opened on 19 July 1900, timed to the World's Fair, with line 1 running from Porte Maillot to Porte de Vincennes. Hector Guimard dressed its entrances in green cast iron grown like plant stems, with amber lamps and lettered signs. He also built covered pavilions with glass roofs, and only two are left. Porte Dauphine still has one where it was built, closed on three sides with enamelled lava panels. The other, the fanned glass canopy at Abbesses, first stood at Hôtel de Ville and was moved up the hill in 1974; Abbesses is on a line built by a rival company that never hired Guimard.
curiosities:Guimard's metro, 1900.why: See both: Porte Dauphine is the one in its original place, Abbesses the one everybody photographs.
facts: Porte Dauphine station (line 2, 16th) and Abbesses station (line 12, 18th); dozens of Guimard's open iron entrances survive elsewhere
Abbesses is usually shown as Montmartre's own Art Nouveau gem; it is a transplant, set on a station Guimard never worked for

curiosities:The Wallace fountains.name: The Wallace fountains
curiosities:The Wallace fountains.teaser: Free drinking water since 1872, from cast-iron fountains painted green so they would blend in
curiosities:The Wallace fountains.story: After the siege of 1870-71 and the Commune, clean water in Paris was scarce and dear. Sir Richard Wallace, an English collector living there, paid for drinking fountains; the first went out in 1872. The large model is cast iron, about 2.7 m tall and close to 600 kg: four caryatids, Kindness, Simplicity, Charity and Sobriety, hold up a dome, and you tell them apart only by a bent knee and the fall of a tunic. They were painted dark green on purpose, to sit quietly among the trees and railings. The thin stream under the dome is the same water as the taps.
curiosities:The Wallace fountains.why: Fill a bottle at one: the water is free and drinkable, and that was the whole point in 1872.
facts: More than a hundred still pour across Paris; fill a bottle from the stream under the dome
The count: the City has given 107 and 109 in recent years, while an older Eau de Paris figure was 155, depending on what is counted

curiosities:Why the bar is called le zin.name: Le zinc is often pewter
curiosities:Why the bar is called le zin.teaser: Parisians meet 'au zinc', at the bar, though many of the old counters are tin alloy
curiosities:Why the bar is called le zin.story: To meet au zinc is to meet at the counter: the metal named the bar. The catch: Many of the old counters you lean on are not zinc but étain, pewter, a tin alloy that 19th-century makers used for bar tops; specialists say they are called zinc wrongly. The second thing to know is on the window. Since a 1987 decree, a café must post outside the prices of its most common drinks both au comptoir and en salle, and the terrace price must be shown as a price, not as a supplement. Standing at the bar is meant to cost less.
curiosities:Why the bar is called le zin.why: Read the price board at the door, then drink your coffee standing at the counter: same cup, lower price.
facts: Any old café counter: run a hand along the rolled edge and read the posted comptoir and salle prices by the door
Why the name stuck: some say early counters were truly zinc-sheathed, specialists say most were pewter from the start

curiosities:Voltaire's forty cups.name: Voltaire's forty cups
curiosities:Voltaire's forty cups.teaser: Voltaire's forty cups a day at Le Procope are a legend; the room's role in café history is real
curiosities:Voltaire's forty cups.story: Le Procope opened in 1686 under Procopio Cutò, an Italian who fitted his rooms with chandeliers, wall mirrors and marble-topped tables, the look Paris cafés would copy. It claims to be the city's oldest café, and La Fontaine, Voltaire, Diderot's Encyclopédistes, Danton and Benjamin Franklin all drank here. Then come the tales. Voltaire is said to have downed some forty cups a day of coffee cut with chocolate; nobody counted. A bicorne in a glass case is said to be the young Napoleon's, left as a pledge for an unpaid bill. The old café closed in 1872; what stands there now has been a restaurant since 1957.
curiosities:Voltaire's forty cups.why: Look in from the Cour du Commerce Saint-André side: the old shopfront on the passage tells the story better than a meal.
facts: 13 Rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, 6th; look in from the Cour du Commerce Saint-André (not a table in this guide)
The forty cups and the hat are house lore, not documented; 'oldest café' holds only if you skip the 85 years it was shut

curiosities:Bistro is not Russian.name: Bistro is not Russian
curiosities:Bistro is not Russian.teaser: The Cossacks shouting 'bystro!' in 1814 is a tale: the word turns up in print some seventy years later
curiosities:Bistro is not Russian.story: Every waiter in Montmartre will tell you: in 1814 Russian soldiers occupying Paris banged the tables and shouted bystro, quickly, and the quick little wine shop got its name. A plaque at La Mère Catherine on Place du Tertre even dates the first cry to 30 March 1814. The trouble is the calendar. The word bistro, or bistrot, does not appear in written French until the 1880s, about seventy years after the Cossacks left. Linguists look instead to regional French: bistraud, a Poitou word for a wine merchant's helper, or bistrouille, rough cheap spirit. None is proven, and the story is too good to die.
curiosities:Bistro is not Russian.why: Tell the Cossack story at the table, then the date that kills it.
facts: The 1814 plaque at La Mère Catherine, Place du Tertre, 18th
The first printed use is put at 1880 or 1884; the real root (bistraud, bistrouille or another regional word) is unsettled

curiosities:Les Halles left in one night.name: The move of the century
curiosities:Les Halles left in one night.teaser: Les Halles did not leave in one night: the 1969 move took several days, and the meat stayed until 1973
curiosities:Les Halles left in one night.story: Zola called Les Halles 'the belly of Paris', and for eight centuries the city's food came through here. The story told everywhere is that it left in a single night. It did not. The 'move of the century' ran over several days at the turn of February and March 1969, some 20,000 people and 1,500 lorries shifting about a thousand wholesalers to Rungis, which opened to buyers on 3 March. The meat traders stayed on until 1973. Baltard's iron pavilions came down in the early 1970s. Today the Forum des Halles and its canopy fill the site, and Saint-Eustache, the market's parish church, still stands over it.
curiosities:Les Halles left in one night.why: Stand by Saint-Eustache and picture the iron halls: the church is the one thing the market porters would still recognise.
facts: Saint-Eustache and the Forum des Halles, 1st; Rungis itself is a professionals' market south of the city
The exact dates (27 Feb to 3 Mar, or 28 Feb to 2 Mar 1969); Rungis is often said to be the world's second-largest wholesale food market after Mexico City's

curiosities:The Paris vineyard.name: The Paris vineyard
curiosities:The Paris vineyard.teaser: Montmartre's vines were replanted in 1933 to stop builders, and the wine is pressed in the town hall
curiosities:The Paris vineyard.story: The Clos Montmartre is the best known of the few vineyards left inside Paris, and it exists because in 1933 the City replanted the slope to keep developers off it. The grapes are picked by hand and pressed in the cellar of the 18th arrondissement's town hall, and the hill yields only about 1,000 to 1,500 bottles a year. Every October since 1934 the harvest is celebrated with the Fête des Vendanges; the 93rd edition ran from 7 to 11 October 2026, with a parade leaving the vines. Otherwise you see it through the railings.
curiosities:The Paris vineyard.why: Walk past the railings on Rue des Saules: a city vineyard on a steep slope above Paris rooftops.
facts: The vines from the street at Rue des Saules and Rue Saint-Vincent, 18th; the Fête des Vendanges each October
The yield is given as 'about a thousand' or 1,000 to 1,500 bottles, depending on the year

curiosities:150 arcades, about 25 left.name: 150 arcades, a handful left
curiosities:150 arcades, about 25 left.teaser: The Right Bank had well over a hundred glass-roofed passages in the 1850s; some twenty to thirty survive
curiosities:150 arcades, about 25 left.story: Before pavements and drains, the glass-roofed passage was how Paris shopped dry-shod: a private lane cut through a block, lit and lined with shops. By the mid-19th century there were around 150 of them on the Right Bank. Then Haussmann's boulevards opened up the quarters, the department stores took the trade, and most were demolished. What is left clusters in the 2nd and 9th arrondissements, near the Grands Boulevards and the Palais-Royal. Passage Jouffroy runs north from Boulevard Montmartre and carries straight on as Passage Verdeau: two passages in a row, a quarter-hour out of the rain.
curiosities:150 arcades, about 25 left.why: Cross Boulevard Montmartre into Passage Jouffroy and keep going through Verdeau: two passages without stepping into the street.
facts: Passage Jouffroy and Passage Verdeau, 9th; Galerie Vivienne and Passage des Panoramas have their own card
The peak (about 150, or 140 per the City) and the survivors (about 20 to 30) depend on what counts as a passage

walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.name: Parc Rives de Seine
walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.teaser: The riverside motorway is gone: both banks are now a car-free walk at water level
walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.story: For decades the Voie Georges-Pompidou welded a motorway to the Right Bank, and on long stretches you simply could not reach the water. Mayor Bertrand Delanoë took back the left bank in 2013, mooring gardens on barges near the Pont de l'Alma; Anne Hidalgo followed on the right bank, opened as a park in 2017, against drivers' groups who fought it in the courts. Now you walk at river level past café terraces and stone steps where Parisians sit with a bottle as the light goes, with the Louvre and the Conciergerie above you and the tour boats passing close enough to wave.
walks:Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free.why: Walk it at dusk from the Orsay end and sit on the steps below the Île de la Cité with the river at your feet.
facts: Below the Musée d'Orsay on the left bank, or the Arsenal marina at the eastern end
Flat paved quays at water level, steps down from the bridges
The floating gardens near the Pont de l'Alma; the right-bank steps facing Île Saint-Louis

secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.name: Square du Vert-Galant
secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.teaser: A willow on the prow of the Île de la Cité, down the steps that most people crossing the Pont Neuf never see
secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.story: Behind the bronze Henri IV on the Pont Neuf, a flight of steps goes down to a small triangular garden at the very tip of the Île de la Cité, close to the river and much lower than the streets above. A weeping willow hangs over the point, a few benches face downstream, and the Seine splits round you on both sides. The garden was made in 1884 by joining silt islets to the island. Its name teases the king overhead: Vert-Galant, the green gallant, for the ageing Henri's long run of mistresses. His Pont Neuf, finished in 1607, is now the oldest bridge standing in Paris.
secret-gems:Square du Vert-Galant.why: Go down at the end of the day and sit on the point under the willow, river on both sides.
facts: Steps down from the Pont Neuf behind the statue of Henri IV, Île de la Cité, 1st
Evening; it can flood when the Seine runs high in winter
The tip of the island under the willow; Place Dauphine just above (its own card)

walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.name: Coulée verte René-Dumont
walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.teaser: A garden on a dead railway viaduct, opened in 1993, sixteen years before New York's High Line
walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.story: Trains ran from Bastille to Vincennes on this line until 1969. Most cities would have pulled the viaduct down; Paris planted it. Landscape architect Jacques Vergely and architect Philippe Mathieux laid a garden along the top, and it opened in 1993, the first elevated railway in the world turned into a park walk. New York's High Line, opened in 2009, cites it as a precedent. The first stretch runs about ten metres up on the brick arches above Avenue Daumesnil, through rose arbours, bamboo and lavender, quiet above the traffic, before dropping to ground level and running on towards the Bois de Vincennes.
walks:Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenad.why: Walk the raised viaduct section from Bastille, then go down to look at the workshops in the arches below.
facts: Behind the Opéra Bastille, by Avenue Daumesnil, 12th

secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.name: La Petite Ceinture
secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.teaser: The railway that once ringed Paris, closed to passengers in 1934 and gone wild in its trench
secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.story: Built from 1852 to carry freight and then passengers round the city inside the old walls, the Petite Ceinture lost its riders to the new métro and closed to passengers in 1934. Then it was left alone. The rails are still in the ballast; buddleia and brambles grow between them, and the 15th-arrondissement stretch alone counts more than 200 wild plant species and some 70 animal species. Of the line's 32 km, the City says 12 to 13 km are now open to walkers. In the 15th a 300 m tunnel has opened between two sections, giving about 2 km continuous from Parc Georges-Brassens to Place Balard.
secret-gems:La Petite Ceinture.why: Go for the strangeness: a railway ruin with foxes and wildflowers, not a manicured park.
facts: Parc Georges-Brassens, 15th, for the longest continuous stretch
About 2 km in the 15th; about 1.6 km in the 12th from Rue de Charenton to Avenue de Saint-Mandé

walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.teaser: Cliffs blasted out of an old gypsum quarry, a lake and a temple on a crag, opened in 1867
walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.story: Few parks in Paris began on worse ground. This was a spent gypsum quarry, a refuse dump and a yard for cutting up horse carcasses, close to the medieval gibbet of Montfaucon, where the bodies of the hanged were left on show. Napoleon III and the engineer Adolphe Alphand turned it into a park for the new working districts: they blasted the quarry into cliffs, filled a lake and crowned a crag of about 50 m with Gabriel Davioud's Temple de la Sibylle, modelled on the one at Tivoli. It opened on 1 April 1867 for the Exposition Universelle.
walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.why: Come for the steep lawns and the cliffs, and look at the temple from across the lake: the island itself is closed.
facts: Entrance at Place Armand-Carrel, by the town hall of the 19th
Steep paths and steps, some sections fenced off

walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.name: Père-Lachaise
walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.teaser: Paris's largest cemetery began empty, until its managers moved in some famous bones
walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.story: Opened in 1804 on the estate of Louis XIV's confessor, Père La Chaise, it drew barely any funerals: too far out of town. So in 1817 the administrators staged a transfer: the supposed remains of Molière and La Fontaine, and the purported remains of the medieval lovers Héloïse and Abélard, laid under a canopy built from salvaged abbey stone. It worked; by 1830 there were more than 33,000 graves. The relics are another matter: historians doubt La Fontaine's body ever left its first grave. Today: 44 hectares of cobbled, chestnut-shaded hillside, cats and moss among the tombs.

walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.teaser: A quiet garden of clipped limes where Paris was called to arms in July 1789
walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.story: Cardinal Richelieu built the palace in the 1630s. A later Duc d'Orléans, short of money, wrapped the garden in arcades of shops to let, and before the Revolution it became the loudest place in Paris: cafés, gambling, pamphlets the police could not touch on the duke's property. At the Café de Foy on 12 July 1789, Camille Desmoulins jumped on a table and called the city to arms, two days before the Bastille fell. In 1985-86, under culture minister Jack Lang, Daniel Buren set 260 black-and-white striped columns in the main courtyard; a national scandal then, a place to sit now.
walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.why: Sit on the fountain rim at lunchtime with the office workers, then cross the Buren columns on the way out.
